la:verb:comito.html:
cŏmĭto, āre, 1, v. a. (poet. collat. form of comitor),
to accompany, attend, follow: quod si Romanae comitarent castra puellae,; ; ; ; : funera, (Att. ap. , is, on account of the corruption of the text, dub.).—
Pass.: comitor, āri,; ; ; .—Esp. freq. in part. perf.: cŏmĭtātus, a, um, accompanied, attended: (mulier) alienis viris comitata,; so with an abl. added, ; ; ; 9, 687; 10, 9; ; ; ; ; : trecentis feminarum comitata,; ; . —As adj.: quod ex urbe parum comitatus exierit,; so, bene,; ; and hence, also, in comp.: puero ut uno esset comitatior,; so ; .

la:adj:comis.gloss: courteous, kind, obliging, affable, gracious, polite
senses: courteous, kind, obliging, affable, gracious, polite
la:adj:comis.html:
cōmis, e, adj.
etym. dub.; cf. concinnus
,
courteous, affable, kind, obliging, friendly, loving (class. in prose and poetry; on account of similarity of meaning, in MSS. very freq. interchanged with communis; hence the readings vary in the best edd.; cf. Drak.; Wolf; Madv.).
Of persons: comes, benigni, faciles, suaves homines esse dicuntur qui erranti comiter monstrant viam (Enn.; cf. under adv.), : illum negat et bonum virum et comem et humanum fuisse, etc., : ego illo usa sum benigno et lepido et comi, (cf. Bentl. N. cr.): comis et humanus,; cf. ; : quis Laelio comior? quis jucundior?: dum illis comis est,; so, bonis (opp. adversus malos injucundus),: comis erga aliquem, (al. communis, but comp. id. Fin. l. l. Madv.): comis in amicitiis tuendis,: in uxorem,: senex comissimus,.—
Of subjects not personal: comi animo,: ingenium,: hospitio,, cf.: vinclum inter hospites comitas, Halm: sermone et congressu,: viā (i. e. more),: oculis alliciendus amor,.—Adv.: cōmĭter, courteously, affably, etc. (very freq.): homo, qui erranti comiter monstrat viam, etc., Enn. ap. ; id. ap. Müll.: facere aliquid,; : appellare unumquemque,: munera missa legatis,; cf. ; : accipere,; ; : invitare regios juvenes,: celebrare regis convivium, (al. leg. comi fronte): administrare provinciam, et saep.; majestatem populi Romani comiter conservato, i. e. willingly, in an obliging, kind manner, a (mildly expressed) formula in treaties of peace, , cf. ; for which, in . imperium majestatemque populi Romani gens Aetolorum conservato sine dolo malo.—Sup., dub. (Ritschl, comptissume).—Comp. apparently not in use.

la:noun:comitium.gloss: A place in the forum where comitia (election assemblies) were held.
senses: A place in the forum where comitia (election assemblies) were held.
la:noun:comitium.html:
cŏm-ĭtĭum, ii, n.
locus a coëundo, id est insimul veniendo, est dictus, Paul. ex Müll.; cf. id.: comitium ab eo quod coibant eo comitiis curiatis, et litium causā
.
In sing., the place for the assembling of the Romans voting by the curiœ situated near the Forum, and separated from it by the ancient Rostra, but sometimes considered as a part of the Forum in a more extended sense (hence, in Dion. Halic. ὁ κράτιστος and ό ἐπιφανέστατος τῆς ἀγορᾶς τόπος): IN COMITIO AVT IN FORO, XII. Tab. ap. ; ; ; ; ; ; ; et saep.; cf. Dict. of Antiq.—
Transf., any place of assembly out of Rome; so of the Ephoreum at Sparta,.—
Trop.: quod (es) esset animi vestibulum et orationis janua et cogitationum comitium,; so, sacri pectoris, Mam. .—
Plur.: cŏmĭtĭa (access. form cŏmĭtĭae, Fratr. Arval. ap. Marin. p. 43; Gloss. Labb. p. 33), the assembly of the Romans for electing magistrates, etc., the comitia.—The comitia were of three kinds.
Comitia curiata, the most ancient, voting by curiæ, held in the comitium (v. I.), gradually restricted by,
The Comitia centuriata, the proper assembly of the populus Romanus, voting by centuries, instituted by Servius Tullius, continuing through the whole time of the republic, commonly held in the Campus Martius (not in the comitium, as is asserted by many from the similarity of the name; cf. campus, II.), sqq.; ; ; ; cf. .—
Comitia tributa, voting by tribes, and commonly held in the Forum, but in choosing magistrates, freq. in the Campus Martius, convened for the first time in the trial of Coriolanus, two years after the introduction of the office of tribune of the people. In them the inferior magistrates (Ædiles, tribunes of the people, quæstors), and, later, the Pontifex Maximus also, were chosen, ; ; ; ; ; cf. Dict. of Antiq.—Upon the comitia calata, v. 1, calo.—The usual t. t. for holding such comitia is: comitia habere,; freq. in all periods; they were designated according to the magistrates who were to be chosen in them, as consularia,; : praetoria,: tribunicia,; : militaria,: quaestoria,; cf. also: comitia consulum,; and: comitia fiunt regi creando,: edicere comitia consulibus creandis,: comitia conficere,: differre,: dimittere,: ducere,: inire,.—
Transf., of other elections, out of Rome, ; ; Tab. Heracl. v. 24 sq.—
Trop.: ibo intro, ubi de capite meo sunt comitia, i. e.,where my fate is deciding,: Pseudulus mihi centuriata capitis habuit comitia,: meo illic nunc sunt capiti comitia,.

la:noun:comitia.gloss: a comitia; a Roman assembly for elections

to offer the sacrifice after which the comitia were held
la:verb:comitio.html:
cŏmĭtĭo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a.
[comitium].
To go into the comitium: quando rex comitiavit, fas (abridged, Q. R. C. F.), an old formula in Müll.; cf. id.; Kalend. Praen. ap. Inscr. Orell. vol. 2, p. 386. —Hence,
cŏmĭtĭātus, i, m., a military tribune elected at the comitia, .

la:noun:comitas.html:
cōmĭtas, ātis, f.
comis
,
courteousness, kindness, obligingness, friendliness, affability, gentleness (syn.: benignitas, facilitas, humanitas; opp. gravitas and severitas; in good prose; esp. freq. in Cic.): si illius (sc. Catonis) comitatem et facilitatem tuae gravitati severitatique asperseris,; ; ; : Crassus in summā comitate habebat etiam severitatis satis, Scaevolae multā in severitate non deerat tamen comitas,; cf. : in socios, mansuetudo in hostes,; ; ; ; ; : comitas affabilitasque sermonis,—
Too great liberality, prodigality, ; ; ; .

la:verb:comitatus.html: cŏmĭtātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from comitor and comito; v. comitor.

senses: an escort or attending multitude, especially an imperial escort or retinue
la:noun:comitatus.html:
cŏmĭtātus, ūs, m.
comes
.
An escort, an attending multitude, a train, retinue (in sing. and plur.).
In gen. (class.): qui cum uxore veheretur in raedā muliebri et delicato ancillarum puerorumque comitatu,: magno comitatu ingredi,: comitatum optimorum civium desero,: praedonis improbissimi societas atque comitatus,; : Pompeius comitatu equitum triginta ad mare pervenit,; ; : iter modico comitatu ingressus est,; et saep.; .—*
Transf., of animals: multo ceterarum volucrum comitatu,.—
Of abstr. objects: pruna hordearia appellata a comitatu frugis ejus,i. e. because they ripen at the same time,; so, virgultorum,: quid tanto virtutum comitatu (opus est) si? etc.,; : utriusque causae,: ferre impetum vitiorum, tam magno comitatu venientium,.—
In partic., in the time of the empire, an imperial escort, retinue, court, suite, ; ; ; ; ; : Osthanes exornatus comitatu Alexandri,honored with the right of attendance upon Alexander,; cf.: deici congressu et comitatu,.—
A company (without the accessory idea of attendance), a band, troop, crowd, swarm: litterae, quaecumque erant in eo comitatu, etc.,; ; ; ; ; ;

la:verb:comitor.gloss: to join someone as an attendant; accompany, attend, follow; guard, escort; serve
senses: to join someone as an attendant; accompany, attend, follow; guard, escort; serve
to attend someone to the grave, attend a funeral
la:verb:comitor.html:
cŏmĭtor, ātus, 1,
v. dep. a. [comes], to join one's self to any one as an attendant, to accompany, attend, follow (class.; esp. freq. after the Aug. per.); constr. with acc. or absol., with abstr. subjects by Cic. three times (qs. comitem esse) with dat. (v. B. β).
In gen.
With acc.: propinqui Indutiomari comitati eos ex civitate excesserunt,: matrem,: patrem,; : nautas fugā,: Metellum in exsilium,: erilem filium in scholas,: hostiam,: iter alicujus,: gressum erilem,: currum Augusti triumpho,; : rem militarem,.—
Absol. (esp. freq. in the Aug. poets and Tac.): lanigerae comitantur oves,; : sex milia Dalmatarum, recens delectus, comitabantur,; ; : non aequo comitantes ordine,; .—In the abl. absol. of the part. pres., with the attendance of, attended by, etc., sometimes to be translated by with, together with, and with a negative, without: magnā comitante catervā,; ; .—In plur., ; ; ; ; : domino comitante,: nupsi non comitante deo, without the assent, against the will of the god (Hymen), . —
Transf. to inanimate objects (cf. comes, I. B.).
With acc.: comitatur fama unionis ejus parem, etc.,: quando comitetur semper artem decor,; cf. also ; ; .—
With dat.: (Tarquinio Superbo) aliquamdiu prospera fortuna comitata est,: tardis enim mentibus virtus non facile comitatur,: cetera, quae comitantur huic vitae,.—
Absol.: an est aliquid per se ipsum flagitiosum, etiam si nulla comitetur infamia?: Teucrum comitantibus armis Punica se quantis attollet gloria rebus!; ; : comitante opinione,.—
In partic., to attend one to the grave: (Eumenem) comitante toto exercitu humaverunt,; : juvenem exanimum vano honore,; cf.: supremum comitentur honorem,.

cōmissātĭo (cōmess-), ōnis, f.
id.
,
a Bacchanalian revel, and the succeeding nocturnal procession with torches and music, a revelling, rioting, ; ; ; ; .—In plur., ; ; Müll.; ; ; ; ; ; .—The tropes tempestas comissationis and comissatio tempestatis are censured, the former as too bold and the latter as too feeble, by Cic., de Or. 3, 41, 164.

la:verb:comissor.html:
cōmissor (on account of erroneous deriv. from comis, comedo, commensa, etc., often written cōmisor, commisor, commissor, cōmesor, cōmes-sor, commessor, commensor, etc.; v. Vel. Long. p. 2233; Drak.; ; Spald. and Zumpt), ātus, 1, v. dep., = κωμάζω (v. Lidd. and Scott in h. v.),
to hold a festive procession, to revel, make merry; of young people, who went about with music and dancing, to celebrate a festival, and finally returned to one of their companions, in order to carouse anew (class.; not in Cic.; cf., however, comissatio and comissator): nunc comissatum ibo ad Philolachetem,: ad fratrem,; : domum,: qui praetereat comissatum volo vocari,, 4, 4: in domum alicujus, * : intromittere aliquam comissatum, * .—Absol.: comissantium modo currum secuti sunt,; * ; ; ; .
